OBSERVATION 2
Procedures to ensure that sampling methods are adequate for their intended use have not been adequately established.
Specifically, the firm’s procedures for establishing sample sizes in validation activities lack clear guidance on when an
external standard (such as an ANSI/ISO sampling requirement) can override or replace the organization’s own internal
criteria. The procedures do not specify the necessary elements such as acceptance criteria, justification, rationale, approval
process, methodology, or how to resolve any conflict between the two sources. Consequently, the choice of sample size in
validation studies may be unsupported by statistical justification and applied inconsistently.
For example: A sample size of six was initially selected in Protocol (DT_DVP0007 01) Manual Cleaning Validation Plan on
the suggestion as per ANSI/AAMI ST98: 2022 [9]. ANSI/AAMI ST98: 2022. This sample size was changed to 9,
a more
conservative sample size, as reflected in the validation report DT_DVROOO7 03 Manual Cleaning Validation Report.
Collectively, these validation reports did not adequately document the following:
e
the factors considered when selecting the initial six-unit size (expert judgment, industry practice, risk assessment,
etc.).
e = the rationale or explanation why a sample size of 9 was sufficient, even if recommended by the standard that
could include a clear, risk-based rationale for the sample size used, is sufficient for the specific device, process and
risk level, and explain the deviation from your own internal SOP.
OBSERVATION 3
The organizational structure has not been adequately established and maintained to ensure that devices are manufactured
in accordance with 21 CFR Part 820.
Specifically, between approximately December 2024 and September 2025, the firm’s approach to managing the quality
system was, in part, triage-oriented rather than maintaining normal quality system operations. The departure of several key
staff members resulted in delays and partial interruptions in the processing of CAPAs, change requests, nonconformances,
and quality plans.
OBSERVATION 4
Process validation activities have not been adequately documented.
Specifically, the stated purpose of the validation protocol (test instructions) RS DVPO0004
"RefluxStop Radiopacity and
Barium Sulphate," was not congruent with the conclusions in the corresponding output report RS DVROO04. The protocol
documentation was inaccurate.

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

deep_analysis_input.body_full: This warning letter advises you of significant deviations identified during a U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) review of records submitted from your facility and provides you the opportunity to address them. Promptly address any deviations described herein without delay, including ensuring that appropriate resources are allocated to fully address them and prevent their recurrence. This is not intended to be an all-inclusive list of the deviations in connection with your products or operations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including FDA regulations. Failure to adequately address any deviations may result in regulatory action without further notice. FDA Review Deviations were documented during review of your drug manufacturing facility, Nanjing Hanxin Pharmaceutical Technology Co. Ltd., FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 3015142388. This review was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. Your facility was registered with the United States FDA as a manufacturer of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). FDA has reviewed the records you submitted in response to our November 18, 2025 request and subsequent correspondence, for records and other information pursuant to section 704(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for your facility. This warning letter summarizes significant deviations from Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) for APIs. Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding of drugs as described in your response to our 704(a)(4) request do not conform to CGMP, your APIs are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). The following deviations were identified during our review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of deviations at your facility. Failure of your quality unit to exercise its responsibility to ensure the APIs manufactured at your facility are in compliance with CGMP. Your firm is a manufacturer of (b)(4) APIs, including (b)(4) APIs. These APIs are for use in further processing to produce sterile drug products and for pharmaceutical compounding operations. Based on the records and information you provided, your quality unit (QU) failed to adequately qualify your suppliers of critical raw materials for the manufacturing of (b)(4) API at your facility. Your firm was (b)(4) based upon an acceptable FDA inspection. Since then, your firm (b)(4) API. However, in your response to our records request for quality information on drugs you produced, you did not provide any documentation with regard to the manufacture of (b)(4) API at your facility. FDA sent a subsequent request for additional information, regarding (b)(4) manufacturing operations at your facility. Your response indicated that after November 2025, the (b)(4) production was moved to a subsidiary of your company, (b)(4) . Your firm qualified (b)(4) as your supplier for (b)(4) , a critical starting material to manufacture (b)(4) API for U.S. distribution. FDA conducted an inspection in (b)(4) and concluded the drugs manufactured by (b)(4) are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B), because of their methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding do not conform to CGMP. Drugs manufactured at (b)(4) were placed on IA 66-40. See FDA Warning Letter (b)(4) 1 issued to (b)(4) for further details. Your oversight of your suppliers is deficient. FDA is also concerned that identifying your firm and not the actual manufacturer of (b)(4) API may have been an attempt to circumvent safeguards associated with the (b)(4) and may pose a risk to consumers of receiving substandard (b)(4) APIs. For manufacturers whose drugs are placed on IA 66-40 for failure to conform to CGMP within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B), FDA has evidence that the drugs listed in the import alerts appear to be adulterated. You are responsible for ensuring that the drugs you receive and distribute are manufactured in compliance with all relevant CGMP requirements for drugs. Up to date information regarding the import alerts can be found at the following FDA website: https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/ialist.html. In response to this letter, provide: A summary of your systemic corrective action and preventive action (CAPA) plan to remediate the supplier qualification program and prevent use of unsuitable material suppliers. A comprehensive assessment and remediation plan to ensure your QU is given the authority and resources to effectively function. The assessment should also include, but not be limited to: o A determination of whether procedures used by your firm are robust and appropriate o Provisions for QU oversight throughout your operations to evaluate adherence to appropriate practices o A complete and final review of each lot and its related information before the QU disposition decision o Oversight and approval of investigations and discharging of all other QU duties to ensure identity, strength, quality, and purity of all products Your stability report and data to support the claimed retest date for all of your APIs intended for U.S. market. A list of all drugs you distributed in the last three years, and the name of the original supplier/manufacturer, or supplier of starting material, such as crude API. For any lots of APIs identified as being produced from materials from a non-compliant supplier/manufacturer, notify your customers in writing, and provide copies of these notifications in response to this letter. Include lot identification and recommended actions in your notifications. Importation of Unapproved Drugs - (b)(4) Your facility lists various APIs under its manufacturer registration that were not referenced in your response to the 704(a)(4) records request but were active under your registration at the time the request was issued, including (b)(4) . Please be advised that (b)(4) is not an API permissible for use in human drug compounding under sections 503A or 503B of the FD&C Act. Conclusion As previously stated, you are responsible for investigating and determining the causes of any deviations and implementing corrective and preventative measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these deviations and any others do not occur. FDA placed all drugs offered for import into the United States from your firm on Import Alert 66-40 on June 22, 2026. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer until any deviations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to any deviations. Failure to address any deviations may also result in the FDA continuing to refuse admission of articles manufactured at Nanjing Hanxin Pharmaceutical Technology Co. Ltd., located at Building C5, No. 9, Weidi Road, Xianlin University Town, Nanjing, Jiangsu into the United States under section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3). Articles under this authority that appear to be adulterated may be detained or refused admission, in that the methods and controls used in their manufacture do not appear to conform to CGMP within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter. Identify your written response with FEI 3015142388 and ATTN: Compliance officer Joan Johnson in the subject line of the email. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your drugs do not deviate from the FD&C Act, include that information for our consideration. FDA post warning letters to www.FDA.gov. **핵심 사실** `근거: 공식 인덱스 + 보조 출처` {{W5}} **시사점** {{W6}} **점검 사항** {{W7}} **출처** 📰 정보출처 [링크](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/compliance-actions-and-activities/warning-letters) · 📎 공식원본 [링크](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/usv-private-limited-735938-11022026)

deep_analysis_input.body_full: FDA Inspection Violations were observed and documented during an inspection of your drug manufacturing facility, USV Private Limited, FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 3004086192, at H-13, 16, 16a, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21 & E-22, OIDC Mahatma Gandhi Udyog Nagar, Dabhel, Daman, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Dam, from April 7 to 17, 2026. This inspection was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. This warning letter summarizes significant violations of Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) regulations for finished pharmaceuticals. See Title 21 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), parts 210 and 211 (21 CFR parts 210 and 211). Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding do not conform to CGMP, your drug products are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). We reviewed your May 8, 2026, response to our Form FDA 483 in detail and acknowledge receipt of your subsequent correspondence. Violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act The following are violations identified during our inspection and review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of violations at your facility. 1. Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures that are designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile, and that include validation of all aseptic and sterilization processes (21 CFR 211.113(b)). Your firm manufactures aseptically filled parenteral (b)(4) drug products. You failed to implement appropriate processes and systems to assure an ongoing state of control of your aseptic processing operations. You aseptically manufacture injectable products using a (b)(4) approach, with (b)(4) . In addition, your (b)(4) filling line included (b)(4) and was intended as a restricted access barrier system (RABS) but had significant design deficiencies. Your airflow visualization studies (i.e., smoke studies) performed for the ISO 5 vial filling line did not exhibit unidirectional airflow throughout the ISO 5 area. This lack of unidirectional airflow poses a significant risk to drug product sterility. For example, airflow was observed to swirl and move upward. Additionally, your smoke studies did not adequately evaluate airflow at ISO 5 to ISO 7 transition interfaces. We also observed poor aseptic technique during (b)(4) interventions on your (b)(4) filling lines. For example, operators breached first air by extending their forearms over sterile equipment. Additionally, there was inadequate control of material flow from ISO 7 to ISO 5 areas. In your response, you acknowledge deficiencies in your aseptic practices and airflow visualization studies. You add that you engaged an independent consultant to advise on these areas. However, your retrospective risk assessment concluded that the process was in a state of control, citing “no growth” (b)(4) monitoring and compliant environmental monitoring for the (b)(4) filling line. You also cite compliant sterility and bacterial endotoxin results for the vial filling line, and passing media fills for (b)(4) lines. Your response is inadequate. The aseptic processing operations have fundamental flaws in design leading to unidirectional airflow deficiencies, poor ergonomics, and deficient aseptic practices. Such inherent flaws cannot be validated and necessitate redesign. While you engaged consultants for specific aspects of your process design and smoke study program, you lack sufficient commitment to comprehensively remediate your aseptic processing operations, supported by a complete assessment of your aseptic processing operation and equipment replacement. Your risk assessment relies on proxy indicators such as sterility results, media fill pass rates, and environmental monitoring data without systematically addressing deficiencies in the design and control of your operation. The ISO 5 area is critical because sterile products are exposed and therefore vulnerable to contamination. Your aseptic manufacturing process should be designed, and operations executed to prevent contamination hazards to your sterile product. In your response to this letter, provide: Your systematic plan to assure adherence to appropriate aseptic practices, cleanroom behavior, and written procedures, including but not limited to an independent assessment of the following with accompanying corrective action and preventive action (CAPA): o Suitability of actual practices based on extensive retrospective review and prospective observation of aseptic processing operations o Deficiencies in production management oversight, and identification of specific improvements to ensure effective and routine supervisory oversight for all batches o Frequency and depth of quality unit (QU) oversight (e.g., audit, ad hoc, daily interactions) of aseptic processing and its support operations o Adequacy of written procedures and operational ergonomics o The assessment should also evaluate how poor aseptic technique and cleanroom behavior may have affected the quality and sterility of your drugs Describe whether all personnel performing activities that take place in ISO 5 areas are held to ISO 5 personnel monitoring standards 2. Your firm failed to have separate or defined areas or such other control systems necessary to prevent contamination or mix-ups. Your firm also failed to use equipment in the manufacture, processing, packing, or holding of drug products that is of appropriate design, adequate size, and suitably located to facilitate operations for its intended use and for its cleaning and maintenance. (21 CFR 211.42(c) and 21 CFR 211.63). Your facilities and equipment are not adequately designed to protect sterile drugs from significant contamination risks. In addition to areas of deficiency described in the first violation in this letter, other examples include: The (b)(4) filling line's (b)(4) conveyor system physically blocked continuous ISO 5 unidirectional airflow from reaching open sterile bottles during transport to the filling station. Critical areas used for aseptic connections, sterile component unwrapping, and material transfers were insufficient to assure maintenance of ISO 5 conditions. Significant turbulence was observed in your vial filling line airflow visualization videos. However, your firm concluded that airflow was adequate. Your initial response indicates that you suspended production on the (b)(4) line, pending engineering assessment and remediation. However, your remediations are minor and narrow in scope. Your response is inadequate because it fails to address the need for comprehensive remediation across your aseptic processing operations. In your response to this letter, provide: Comprehensive, independent risk assessment of all contamination hazards with respect to your aseptic processes, equipment, and facilities, including but not limited to: o All human interactions within the ISO 5 area (e.g., risk reduction or elimination of (b)(4) interventions wherever possible) o Equipment suitability (e.g., reliability, capability, ergonomics, placement) and sufficient cleanroom space o Air quality in the ISO 5 area and surrounding room including, but not limited to, air volume and flow o Facility layout o Personnel Flow and Material Flow (movement throughout all rooms used to conduct and support sterile operations, and all material transfers) o Specific CAPA recommendations that will comprehensively address the design and control hazards identified in the risk assessment o A detailed remediation plan with timelines to address the findings of the contamination hazards risk assessment. Describe specific tangible improvements to be made to aseptic processing operation design and control at your facility and explain how this CAPA plan will robustly remediate your deficient sterile manufacturing operations. Include comprehensive changes to the design of both your aseptic processing lines and cleanrooms. Also, describe your plans for qualification and validation of your extensively remediated operations. o Also describe your contingency plans in the event your supply chain continuity may be compromised (e.g., stockpiling inventory using interim manufacturing controls, and/or utilizing contract manufacturing organizations). An independent, comprehensive evaluation of airflow unidirectionality in your aseptic processing operations. Ensure smoke studies are conducted under dynamic conditions with thorough and complete evaluations of aseptic processing line airflow unidirectionality, including special emphasis on the impact of aseptic interventions and dynamic interactions with the surrounding cleanroom. Conduct these smoke studies after you remediate your aseptic operation and using proper practices (e.g., neutrally buoyant media) to appropriately visualize airflow. For your aseptic processing rooms, provide detailed description of the current location of each air return, including but not limited to any located on or near the ceiling. Describe in detail the air flow dynamics at each return and provide any related smoke studies. Your CAPA plan to implement routine, vigilant operations management oversight of facilities and equipment. This plan should incorporate oversight from a qualified independent consultant and ensure, among other things, prompt detection of equipment/facilities performance issues, effective execution of repairs, adherence to appropriate preventive maintenance schedules, timely technological upgrades to the equipment/facility infrastructure, and improved systems for senior management review. Your plan should also ensure that appropriate actions are taken throughout the company network. 3. Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures designed to assure that components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling, and drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)). Your visual inspection program was inadequate to assure your drug products were essentially free of visible particulates. Lack of Alert and Action Limits You lacked action limits for visible particulates. You also only defined alert limits for certain particulate types in selected presentations of your (b)(4) injection drug products. Your visual inspection procedure requires the investigation of atypical trends, yet you failed to investigate atypical trends in (b)(4) injection batch (b)(4) . Without well-defined metrics to characterize acceptable process performance, including but not limited to alert and action limits, it is difficult to reliably detect when a process has deviated from a state of control. Lack of Extrinsic and Intrinsic Particulate Classification You did not classify particulates as extrinsic or intrinsic. However, your procedures state that extrinsic particulates indicating filth, sterility assurance issues, or CGMP violations are unacceptable irrespective of statistical sampling acceptance criteria. Your failure to classify extrinsic particles from your batches can lead to not detecting critical quality and safety risks. Prior to March 28, 2026, you also released all batches of (b)(4) without adequate visible particulate assessment. In your response, you commit to establish alert and action limits for all products. You also commit to implement intrinsic and extrinsic particulate classifications, and a destructive testing program for (b)(4) containers (such as those used for (b)(4) . You state that retrospective destructive testing of (b)(4) batches within expiry did not detect any particles. Your response is inadequate. It does not address your failure to follow your own procedures on batch disposition criteria for extrinsic particles for products already distributed. Moreover, retrospective destructive testing and assessments of flawed visual inspection data cannot substitute for the required characterization and control you lacked at the time of production. In response to this letter, provide: Raw data and tabulated summary of your retrospective destructive testing results An independent, comprehensive assessment and remediation plan for your visual inspection program to ensure compliance with CGMP. The remediation plan should incorporate USP <790> Visible Particulates in Injections (b)(4) , including container-specific testing protocols (e.g., (b)(4) containers) for each container type. Your strategy should include: o For all products, assess the suitability of all specifications, alert and action limits, sampling methods, test methods, and validation for visible particulate inspection, subvisible particulate inspection, as well as any supplemental destructive tests, to determine if they are sufficient to support batch disposition decisions. The assessment should also identify appropriate CAPAs, including these elements:  Enhancements to your 100% visible particulate inspection practices to improve detectability and reliability  Robust methods, equipment, and personnel qualifications to reproducibly detect visible particulates  Rigorous qualification studies to ensure your (b)(4) visible particulate inspection systems consistently and reproducibly detect the variety of visible particulates encountered in your drug products  Review past history to develop a product-specific, risk-based visual inspection approach incorporating product knowledge, process experience, deviation investigation analysis, historical data on particle contaminants and sources, and recall/complaint data to ensure ongoing compliance with USP <790>, (b)(4) , and CGMP requirements o If you manufacture difficult-to-inspect products (e.g., (b)(4) containers), address these elements and provide a CAPA:  100% visible inspection using enhanced lighting with background contrast methods, as appropriate (e.g., (b)(4) containers (b)(4) ) that optimize visual inspection  Identify provisions for highly capable supplemental destructive testing and/or use of advanced technologies (e.g., (b)(4) ), as appropriate, with statistically significant sample sizes to test for critical defects. o If you manufacture drug products that preclude visual particulate inspection (e.g., products packaged in (b)(4) containers), address these elements and provide a CAPA:  Highly capable destructive testing method(s), with appropriate, statistically significant sample sizes to test for particulates. o In each case, whenever visual inspection methods are insufficient or cannot be used, also implement enhanced upstream particulate controls (e.g., in-process (b)(4) , environmental controls, protective design provisions, robust container/closure supplier oversight). This should also generally include appropriate in-process visible particulate matter testing at (b)(4) stage. o A risk assessment of all previously released batches currently within expiry that were released without adequate evaluation of particulate contamination. A comprehensive, independent assessment of your overall system for investigating deviations, discrepancies, complaints, out-of-specification results, action level results (out of limits), and failures. Provide a detailed action plan to remediate this system. Your action plan should include, but not be limited to, significant improvements in investigation competencies, scope determination, root cause evaluation, CAPA effectiveness, QU oversight, and written procedures. Address how your firm will ensure all phases of investigations are appropriately conducted. A comprehensive assessment and remediation plan to ensure your QU is given the authority, independence, and resources to effectively function that includes, but is not limited to: o A determination of whether procedures used by your firm are robust and appropriate o Provisions for independent QU oversight throughout your operations to ensure satisfactory procedures and adherence to appropriate practices o A complete and final review of each batch and its related information before the QU disposition decision o Oversight and approval of investigations and discharging of all other QU duties to ensure identity, strength, quality, and purity of all products o Also, describe how executive management will support robust quality assurance at your firm, including but not limited to timely provision of resources that enable proactive detection and resolution of emerging manufacturing/quality issues to assure a continuing state of control Visible Particulate Contamination We encourage the use of suitable (b)(4) visual inspection for particulates to augment the (b)(4) visual inspection program. (b)(4) methods should be rigorously studied, and qualified, to assess their capability and robustness under various conditions, machine settings, container-closure sizes, defect types, product characteristic, and other variables. In addition, any use of (b)(4) particulate inspection as an adjunct method does not supplant the need for (b)(4) visual inspection for various other attributes (e.g., cracks, deformities, closure issues, volume, insufficient (b)(4) , leaks, (b)(4) , discoloration, turbidity, other appearance defects). It is important that any visible particulate contamination is appropriately evaluated and investigated. Visible particulates in injectable products should be avoided through appropriate preventive measures built into your design and production controls. When categorizing any visible particles, extrinsic or foreign matter should receive special attention, as it may indicate possible microbial contamination. Extrinsic or foreign particulate contamination should occur very infrequently, and trigger a thorough investigation and appropriate CAPA. (b)(4) product operations should be designed to prevent particle contamination. Regarding (b)(4) products, it is essential that operations are designed and controlled to protect consumers from the risk of (b)(4) potentially harmful particles (b)(4) . Microbes introduced (b)(4) can pose a serious risk to consumers. Irreversible damage, including (b)(4) , can occur and, in some cases, may progress to life-threatening systemic infection. Additional Guidance on Aseptic Processing See FDA’s guidance document Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing—Current Good Manufacturing Practice to help you meet the CGMP requirements when manufacturing sterile drugs using aseptic processing at https://www.fda.gov/media/71026/download. Quality Systems Your firm’s quality systems are inadequate. For guidance on establishing and maintaining CGMP-compliant quality systems, see FDA guidances: Q8(R2) Pharmaceutical Development at https://www.fda.gov/media/71535/download, Q9(R1) Quality Risk Management at https://www.fda.gov/media/167721/download, and Q10 Pharmaceutical Quality System at https://www.fda.gov/media/71553/download. Significant findings in this letter demonstrate that your firm does not operate an effective quality system in accord with CGMP. In addition to the lack of effective management oversight of your production operations, we found your QU is not enabled to exercise proper authority and/or has insufficiently implemented its responsibilities. Executive management should immediately and comprehensively assess your company’s global manufacturing operations to ensure that your systems, processes, and products conform to FDA requirements. Drug Production Suspended We acknowledge your initial commitment to suspend production of your (b)(4) drugs at this facility for the U.S. market. You subsequently notified us of your decision to discontinue commercial manufacturing of product from the (b)(4) filling line to the U.S. market. In response to this letter, clarify whether you intend to resume manufacturing (b)(4) drugs for the U.S. market at this facility in the future. If you plan to resume any manufacturing operations regulated under the FD&C Act, notify this office before resuming your drug manufacturing operations. If you resume CGMP activities, you are responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure your firm is capable of ongoing CGMP compliance. In addition, based upon the nature of the violations we identified at your firm, you should engage a consultant qualified as set forth in 21 CFR 211.34 to assist your firm in meeting CGMP requirements. The qualified consultant should also perform a comprehensive six-system audit 1 of your entire operation for CGMP compliance and evaluate the completion and efficacy of all corrective action and preventive action, before you pursue resolution of your firm’s compliance status with FDA. Your use of a consultant does not relieve your firm’s obligation to comply with CGMP. Your firm’s executive management remains responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure ongoing CGMP compliance. In your notification to the Agency, provide a summary of your remediations to demonstrate that you have appropriately completed all CAPA. Conclusion You are responsible for investigating and determining the root causes of any violations and implementing corrective and preventative measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these violations and any others do not occur. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer until any violations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may re-inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to any violations. Failure to address any violations may also result in the FDA refusing admission of articles manufactured at USV Private Limited, Dabhel, Daman, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Dam, India, into the United States under section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3). Articles under this authority that appear to be adulterated may be detained or refused admission, in that the methods and controls used in their manufacture do not appear to conform to CGMP within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). If you are considering an action that is likely to lead to a disruption in the supply of drugs produced at your facility, FDA requests that you contact CDER’s Drug Shortages Staff immediately, at drugshortages@fda.hhs.gov, so that FDA can work with you on the most effective way to bring your operations into compliance with the law. Contacting the Drug Shortages Staff also allows you to meet any obligations you may have to report discontinuances or interruptions in your drug manufacture under 21 U.S.C. 356C(b). This also allows FDA to consider, as soon as possible, what actions, if any, may be needed to avoid shortages and protect the health of patients who depend on your products. Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter. 2 Identify your written response with FEI 3004086192 and ATTN: William Yang in the subject line of the email. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov. Sincerely, /S/ Francis Godwin Director Office of Manufacturing Quality Office of Compliance Center for Drug Evaluation and Research U.S. Food and Drug Administration cc: Registered U.S. Agent Vikas Yadav Pharmavector LLC (b)(4) _______________________ 1 i.e. Quality System, Facilities & Equipment System, Materials System, Production System, Packaging & Labeling System, and Laboratory Control System per FDA’s guidance document Quality Systems Approach to Pharmaceutical CGMP Regulations. 2 Under program enhancements for the Generic Drug User Fee Amendments (GDUFA) reauthorization for fiscal years (FYs) 2023-2027, also known as the GDUFA III Commitment Letter, your facility may be eligible for a Post-Warning Letter Meeting to obtain preliminary feedback from FDA on the adequacy and completeness of your corrective action plans. wl_violation_translation_input.statement: Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures that are designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile, and that include validation of all aseptic and sterilization processes (21 CFR 211.113(b)).

Your firm failed to have separate or defined areas or such other control systems necessary to prevent contamination or mix-ups. Your firm also failed to use equipment in the manufacture, processing, packing, or holding of drug products that is of appropriate design, adequate size, and suitably located to facilitate operations for its intended use and for its cleaning and maintenance. (21 CFR 211.42(c) and 21 CFR 211.63).

Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures designed to assure that components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling, and drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)).

1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or

Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

deep_analysis_input.body_full: This warning letter advises you of a significant violation identified during a U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) review of records from your facility and provides you the opportunity to address them. This is not intended to be an all-inclusive list of violations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including FDA regulations. Failure to adequately address any violations may result in regulatory action without further notice. Your facility, Tianjin Healthcare Medical Technology Co., Ltd. (hereafter THM), FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) # 3015495180 at 2-2066, No 88 HuanHe South Road, Tianjin Free Trade Pilot Zone, KongGang Economic Zone, Tianjin is registered with the FDA as a manufacturer of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). A review of import records showed multiple shipments of APIs intended for pharmacy compounding into the U.S., which declared THM, as the drug manufacturer. The FDA sent requests for records and other information, pursuant to section 704(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 21 U.S.C. 374(a)(4), to the contact email address provided in your registration file. Your firm refused to provide the duly requested records. It is a prohibited act under section 301(e) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 331(e)) to refuse to permit access to or copying of any record as required by section 704(a). Because your firm failed to respond to the section 704(a)(4) records requests and associated communication attempts, we have no indication of the level of quality assurance for drugs listed as manufactured at your facility. Refusal to Provide Records On June 17, 2026, the FDA sent an electronic records request to the contact email address provided in your registration file. You replied on June 24, 2026, that you would “discontinue the production of relevant (b)(4) products” for the U.S. market and refused to provide the requested documents. A follow up request was sent on June 25, 2026, informing you that APIs your firm manufactured were imported to the U.S. market and were still within expiry. Therefore, the requested records were still required. You responded that you would not provide the requested records. Simply ceasing commercial distribution or expressing an intent to stop production does not retroactively relieve you of your regulatory obligations. FDA placed all drugs and drug products offered for import into the U.S. from your firm on Import Alert 66-79 on August 25, 2026. If you no longer intend to manufacture or distribute drug products for the U.S. market, you must formally update your registration and drug listings to reflect this change in operations. Pursuant to 21 CFR 207.29(a)(3), an establishment must update its registration within 30 calendar days of ceasing operations. Conclusion The violation cited in this letter is not intended to be an all-inclusive list of violations at your facility. Until FDA is able to confirm compliance with CGMP and other applicable requirements, we may withhold approval of any new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer. In addition, shipments of articles manufactured at THM, 2-2066, No 88 HuanHe South Road, Tianjin Free Trade Pilot Zone, KongGang Economic Zone, Tianjin into the U.S. that appear to be adulterated or misbranded are subject to being detained or refused admission pursuant to section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3). In response to this letter, you may submit a request to schedule an FDA inspection. Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter. Identify your written response with FEI 3015495180 and ATTN: Marva Taylor in the letter in the subject line of the email. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov. Sincerely, /S/ Francis Godwin Director Office of Manufacturing Quality Office of Compliance Center for Drug Evaluation and Research U.S. Food and Drug Administration cc: U.S. agent (b)(6) Content current as of: 11/10/2026 Regulated Product(s) Drugs Feedback FDA Archive About FDA Accessibility Visitor Information Website Policies / Privacy No FEAR Act Vulnerability Disclosure Policy FOIA HHS.gov USA.gov Contact FDA Follow FDA on Facebook Follow FDA on X Follow FDA on Instagram Follow FDA on LinkedIn View FDA videos on YouTube Subscribe to FDA RSS feeds Contact Number 1-888-INFO-FDA (1-888-463-6332) Back to Top

rows.body: Geneva, 12 November 2026: The PIC/S Committee adopted the revised Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme (PIC/S 1/95 (Rev. 7)) at its meeting on 2 November 2026 in Istanbul, Türkiye. The revised Scheme entered into force on the same date. The PIC Scheme serves as the legal basis and institutional framework for PIC/S as a non-profit association established under Swiss law. It governs the organisation and functioning of PIC/S and establishes a legally non-binding arrangement for co-operation between its Members. Unlike the Pharmaceutical Inspection Convention of 1970, which is an international treaty providing for mutual recognition of inspections, the PIC Scheme offers a flexible framework for international regulatory co-operation. Established in 1995, PIC/S core mission is to lead the international development, implementation, and maintenance of harmonised GMP standards and quality systems of Inspectorates in the field of medicinal products. The previous revision of the PIC Scheme was adopted in November 2019. The current revision introduces significant updates to modernise the institutional and governance framework of PIC/S, reflect the evolution of its activities and strengthen its capacity to fulfil its public health mission. The main changes introduced by Revision 7 include: Reinforcing PIC/S' mission and strategic objectives: explicitly placing the protection of public health at the centre of its mission and strengthening the emphasis on inspection reliance, global regulatory convergence and co-operation with international regulatory and harmonisation bodies. Clarifying membership categories and requirements: introducing Participating Organisations as a distinct membership category, subject to specific PIC/S requirements, and updating relevant definitions and terminology. Strengthening training and knowledge sharing: reinforcing the role of the PIC/S Inspectorates' Academy (PIA) in promoting harmonised training, consistent inspector qualification processes and inspection excellence, while supporting structured knowledge transfer and capacity building. Modernising governance arrangements: clarifying the respective responsibilities, delegation of powers and oversight arrangements of the PIC/S Committee, Executive Bureau and Secretariat, including the management of the Secretariat. Enhancing financial governance and accountability: updating provisions relating to financial oversight, the review of annual accounts and auditing arrangements, in accordance with the applicable Swiss legal framework. The revised PIC Scheme (PIC/S 1/95 (Rev. 7)) is available on the PIC/S website under Publications Link.

rows.body: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is partially granting a color additive petition submitted by Environmental Defense Fund et al. (petitioners), by amending our color additive regulations, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, to remove the authorized use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. The petitioners provided data demonstrating that this additive induces cancer in laboratory animals. We are denying the remaining petition requests to remove ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene from the list of authorized extraction solvents for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin, because any residue of the solvent would be an impurity in the color additive and such impurities are not subject to the Delaney Clause.

rows.body: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is partially granting a color additive petition submitted by the International Association of Color Manufacturers (IACM or petitioner), by amending our color additive regulations, on the basis of abandonment, to remove the authorized uses of methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride from the list of authorized extraction solvents for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin. The petitioner provided data demonstrating that these uses have been permanently abandoned. FDA is denying as moot the portion of the petition proposing that the color additive regulations be amended, on the basis of abandonment, to no longer authorize the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. This request is moot because the authorization for this use has been removed, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, in response to a separate petition.

rows.body: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or Agency) is announcing the availability of a draft guidance for industry titled "Early-Phase IND Protocol Recommendations for Solid Tumors." The purpose of this draft guidance is to provide recommendations to sponsors and clinical investigators developing early-phase trials, which include first-in- human (FIH) protocols or protocols for drugs and biologic products with limited human experience, submitted under an Investigational New Drug Application (IND) to the appropriate disease-specific division located within the Office of Oncologic Diseases (OOD) in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) and the Office of Clinical Evaluation (OCE) in the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER.) This draft guidance is specific to solid tumors and does not address protocols for investigational drugs intended to treat hematologic malignancies.

Interested parties may include regulated industry, health information technology (HIT) vendors, academic medical centers, electronic data capture vendors, patient advocates, and other interested parties.
